title: Discovering Opinion Intervals from Conflicts in Signed Graphs
paper_category: cs.SI (signed graphs / social network analysis, with theory in cs.DS)

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Theorem 2.2 (Revised) states 'the proposed reduction does not guarantee an equivalence between acyclic partitions and conflict-free interval representations' and that 'the NP-hardness claim for BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION remains open under the current construction'. This directly contradicts (a) the immediately following paragraph, which derives inapproximability and no-FPT consequences from the theorem; (b) Appendix A.3, which proves both directions of the reduction and ends 'completing the proof of Theorem 2.2'; (c) the Introduction ('we show that BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION is NP-hard even when... G+ forms a cycle'); and (d) the Conclusion ('We gave strong hardness results'). The appendix proof itself was checked and is sound, so the disclaiming theorem statement is the inconsistent element.

predicted_errors.error_location: Whole paper: Abstract, Section 2.1, Section 2.2, Section 4, Section 5, Appendices A-B
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper simultaneously claims and disclaims both of its central theoretical results. Hardness: NP-hardness is asserted (Introduction, Conclusion, implications paragraph) and fully proved (Appendix A), yet declared 'open' (Theorem 2.2 Revised) and 'flawed' (Conclusion paragraph 2). PTAS: Theorem 2.3 asserts an unconditional (1+eps)-approximation proved in Appendix B, yet Section 2.2 says 'the general case requires further algorithmic innovations beyond current methods' and the Abstract says 'comprehensive theoretical guarantees remain an open challenge'.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4 Experiments (setup paragraph vs RQ3; RQ2 vs Table 7)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The setup paragraph claims 'We do not vary or adapt interval architectures to examine their impact on solution quality', while the RQ3 paragraph in the same section reports running the algorithms with 4, 8, 12, and 16 intervals (Figure 3b), and Appendix Table 3 tabulates the full 4/8/12/16-chain sweep on all 8 datasets. Additionally, RQ2 claims 'some instances requiring hours to reach near-stationary solutions', which is incompatible with Table 7 (worst convergence time 1470 s ~ 24.5 min over 50 runs on all datasets) and the hard 30-minute timeout specified in Appendix C.2.

Section 2.2 states 'while a PTAS is feasible for limited and well-structured interval overlaps, the general case requires further algorithmic innovations beyond current methods' and that overlapping intervals make 'greedy assignments approximate at best'. This contradicts Theorem 2.3 in the same section (an unconditional PTAS for all complete graphs and fixed k, runtime 2^{O(k^2 log(k/(eps delta))/eps^3)} n) and Appendix B, which proves it via Proposition B.1 and Corollary B.2 with verified arithmetic.

Consecutive paragraphs contradict each other: 'We gave strong hardness results for incomplete graphs, as well as a PTAS for complete graphs and fixed k' vs 'given the flaws identified in the current hardness proofs and the limitations of PTAS applicability, foundational understanding of BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION remains incomplete'. No flaws are identified anywhere in the appendices, whose proofs are complete.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4, RQ2 (Computational efficiency) vs Table 7 and Appendix C.2
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: RQ2 states 'some instances requiring hours to reach near-stationary solutions'. Table 7 reports the worst convergence time across all 50 runs and all 8 datasets as 1470.0 s (~24.5 minutes, WikiConflict GAIA), and Appendix C.2 specifies termination 'after 30 minutes by timeout', making multi-hour runs impossible under the reported protocol.

The Abstract describes 'preliminary hardness results' and says 'comprehensive theoretical guarantees remain an open challenge', while the body states and fully proves an NP-hardness theorem (Appendix A) and a PTAS with an explicit (1+eps) guarantee (Theorem 2.3, Appendix B), which the Conclusion calls 'strong hardness results'.

Figure 4's caption asserts 'Negative numbers indicate an improvement over the ground truth... [the algorithms] find alternative, better solutions in sparse graphs', while the RQ5 text asserts the opposite interpretation of the same data: 'observed negative normalized disagreement differences likely arise from optimization noise or overfitting to sampled edges, rather than genuine improvements beyond ground truth'. These readings are mutually exclusive: an assignment with a strictly better objective value than the planted assignment is, by definition of the objective, a genuine improvement over the ground truth.

summary: Exhaustive verification (strict sensitivity) of all 74 snippets found a consistent pattern of high-confidence internal contradictions: the paper claims and simultaneously disclaims both of its central theoretical results. Theorem 2.2 (Revised) declares the NP-hardness reduction inconclusive and the hardness claim 'open', yet the Introduction, the implications paragraph, the Conclusion, and a complete (and independently verified sound) proof in Appendix A all assert and establish the result; likewise, Section 2.2 and the Abstract hedge that the PTAS/theoretical guarantees 'remain an open challenge' while Theorem 2.3 and Appendix B state and prove an unconditional PTAS with verified constants. The Experiments section contradicts itself (claiming interval architectures were never varied while RQ3 and Appendix Table 3 report a full 4/8/12/16-interval sweep) and contradicts its own runtime data (claiming 'hours' of convergence versus a measured maximum of 24.5 minutes and a 30-minute timeout), and the RQ5 text reverses the interpretation stated in Figure 4's caption. In contrast, the quantitative backbone of the paper is clean: all mathematics checked out (Chernoff/sample-size arithmetic in Lemma B.3, telescoping bound in Lemma B.4, the explicit interval construction in Appendix A.3, and all five structural lemmas), every cross-table number is internally consistent (Tables 1/4, 5/6, and 2 agree exactly; the 38% average improvement is correct), and all spot-checked citations are real and correctly attributed. The erratum-worthy defects are the self-contradictory claim-status statements, which appear injected into an otherwise coherent paper; a correction should restore consistent claims for Theorems 2.2/2.3 and remove the contradicting experiment statements. Figures could not be pixel-verified (image files absent); two sub-threshold observations (Figure 8 member counts summing to ~2600 vs |V|=1480, and interval 3's SPD membership differing between Figure 1's caption and Figure 8's table) were noted at confidence 0.6 and excluded.
